articles.title: America Will Soon Let You Pay $750 to Skip the Visa Line. India's Travellers Are the Obvious Customer.
articles.excerpt: A six-month State Department pilot starting July 1 lets visitor-visa applicants buy an interview within 10 business days — a paid fast lane in a system where Indians have long waited months for a slot.
articles.image_caption: The U.S. Embassy in New Delhi; a new State Department pilot offers Indian travellers faster visa interviews for a fee
articles.nri_angle: Indians generate some of the world's heaviest demand for US visitor visas and have long faced months-long appointment backlogs, so a paid fast lane offering an interview within 10 business days — for USD 750 on top of the USD 185 fee — lands squarely on the diaspora's frequent fliers, from parents visiting grandchildren to founders and professionals shuttling across the India-US corridor.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After a Decade of Waiting, India's Biggest Stock Exchange Is Finally Going Public. The Owner of the Market Is About to Join It.
articles.excerpt: The National Stock Exchange has filed for a roughly Rs 30,000-crore offer-for-sale — set to be India's largest-ever IPO — at a valuation near $55 billion, ending a listing saga that has dragged since 2016.
articles.image_caption: The National Stock Exchange building in Mumbai; NSE has filed for what would be India's largest-ever IPO
articles.nri_angle: NRIs increasingly route remittances and savings into Indian equities and index funds, and the NSE IPO offers a chance to own a piece of the marketplace itself — a stock that has been off-limits until now — with eligible NRIs able to apply via NRE/NRO portfolio accounts, while the back-to-back NSE and Jio mega-listings signal the deepening of the very markets the diaspora uses to keep financial roots at home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adani Is Betting $2 Billion That the Next City Grows Around the Airport, Not the Other Way Around
articles.excerpt: The group's airports arm will build 'airport cities' — hotels, offices, retail and entertainment — across more than 655 acres at six Indian airports, modelled on Singapore, Dubai and Amsterdam.
articles.image_caption: An airport terminal in India; Adani Airports plans 'airport cities' across six Indian airports
articles.nri_angle: NRIs experience India most often through its airports, and Adani's $2 billion bet on 'airport cities' at Mumbai, Ahmedabad and four other hubs means more hotels, business space and world-class terminals for diaspora travellers — while reshaping the earnings of a group that is a fixture of NRI investment portfolios directly and through Indian index funds.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After Three Years of Talks, the India-UK Trade Deal Finally Goes Live July 15 — and It Quietly Rewrites the Rules for Indian Workers Abroad
articles.excerpt: Cheaper Scotch and British cars grab the headlines, but the deal's real prize for the diaspora is a pact that spares some 75,000 Indian professionals from paying into two countries' social-security systems at once.
articles.image_caption: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal, in London for talks before the India-UK trade deal takes effect July 15
articles.nri_angle: For Britain's 1.9-million-strong Indian community — the country's largest ethnic-minority group — the deal cuts tariffs that touch NRI-run import, restaurant and textile businesses, eases visas for chefs, yoga teachers and musicians, and, most importantly, ends the double social-security charge on the roughly 75,000 Indian professionals seconded to the UK who until now paid into two pension systems while collecting from one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Twin Earthquakes Devastate Venezuela Near Caracas, Killing Scores — and the Shock Reaches India's Oil Bill
articles.excerpt: Two powerful quakes struck barely 39 seconds apart, flattening buildings in a country already hollowed out by years of crisis, while a jump in crude prices ripples toward import-dependent India.
articles.image_caption: Caracas, Venezuela; twin earthquakes near the capital have left thousands feared dead
articles.nri_angle: A catastrophe in Venezuela reaches Indians on two fronts — the long-rooted Indian-origin communities across the Caribbean and Latin America with relatives and businesses in the region, and the wider economy at home, where a quake-driven rise in global crude prices lifts the import bill of a country that buys more than 85% of its oil abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Financial-Crime Agency Raided the World's Biggest Gold Processor. The Books Allegedly Didn't Match the Vault.
articles.excerpt: After SEBI accused Rajesh Exports of inflating revenue by an almost unimaginable Rs 15.15 lakh crore, investigators found the physical gold was 40% short of what the ledgers claimed — and money trails running to the UAE and African mines that no one can fully account for.
articles.image_caption: Refined gold bars; the ED found Rajesh Exports' physical gold stock about 40% short of its books
articles.nri_angle: Through its Shubh Jewellers chain and the Valcambi refinery — a globally trusted source of minted gold bars and coins — Rajesh Exports sits close to the supply chain NRIs buy from for weddings, festivals and savings, so allegations that a marquee Indian gold name fabricated revenue on a record scale, routed metal through suspicious UAE channels and came up 40% short on physical stock strike directly at the diaspora's confidence in the integrity of Indian gold and in the Indian equities and jewellery brands many of them invest in.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Fire at a Tata Data Centre in Delhi May Have Erased 20 Years of One Company's Data. Google Cloud Was Hit Too.
articles.excerpt: A June 5 blaze at the STT-Tata facility in Greater Kailash caused 'extensive damage,' and three weeks on the recovery is still failing — a warning about how much of digital India sits in a handful of buildings.
articles.image_caption: Server racks inside a data centre; a June 5 fire at the STT-Tata facility in Delhi caused extensive damage
articles.nri_angle: NRIs depend on Indian cloud and telecom infrastructure daily — from international SIMs and remittance apps to the e-governance portals used to renew OCI cards, file taxes and manage NRI accounts — so a Delhi data-centre fire that may have destroyed 20 years of one firm's records and disrupted Google Cloud across India is a direct warning about how concentrated, and how fragile, the digital systems holding diaspora documents and money can be.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Gold Just Broke Below $4,000 for the First Time Since November. It's Down a Quarter From Its Peak.
articles.excerpt: A surging dollar, a Fed suddenly talking about rate hikes and fading Iran-war fears have wiped roughly 25% off gold since January — and India's own effort to defend the rupee by curbing gold imports is quietly part of the story.
articles.image_caption: Gold bullion bars; spot gold fell below $4,000 an ounce for the first time since November 2025
articles.nri_angle: Gold is the asset class woven into diaspora weddings, festivals and family savings, and NRIs are among the world's most active cross-border gold buyers — so a 25% crash from January's record reshapes their calculations at once: paper losses for recent buyers, a first real buying window before Diwali for those holding cash, and a stronger dollar that stretches remittances further in rupees even as the gold those rupees buy has cheapened.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Canada Has a Message for Indian Students: This Is the 'Best Time Ever' to Apply.
articles.excerpt: As the US dangles visa expiry dates and Australia doubles its fees, Canada's envoy in Delhi insists the doors never closed — the student caps aren't even full, and Ottawa wants Indians to come.
articles.image_caption: A Canadian university campus; Canada's envoy says it is the 'best time ever' for Indian students to apply
articles.nri_angle: Study abroad is one of the largest financial and emotional decisions Indian families make and often the first foothold for a new branch of the diaspora; with the US, UK, Canada and Australia all tightening at once, an explicit invitation from Canada's envoy — caps unfilled and doors open — is significant for the lakhs of students choosing a destination, even as recent approval data and a warming India-Canada relationship counsel reading the welcome in full.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Amazon Just Doubled Down on India. It's Putting Another $13 Billion Into AI and the Cloud.
articles.excerpt: The fresh commitment, announced Thursday, lifts Amazon's planned India spending to nearly $50 billion by 2030 — a vote of confidence in the country's data-centre boom that the diaspora's engineers and small businesses will feel directly.
articles.image_caption: An Amazon Web Services data centre; AWS anchors Amazon's expanded AI and cloud investment in India
articles.nri_angle: Amazon's additional $13 billion India investment — lifting its planned spend to nearly $50 billion by 2030 — deepens the country's AI and cloud capacity, creating senior technical roles at home that strengthen the case for diaspora reverse-migration, lowering costs for diaspora-founded startups that build on AWS, and promising affordable AI tools to millions of small Indian businesses with relatives abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Has Run Out of EB-2 Green Cards for Indians This Year. The Wait Now Stretches to October.
articles.excerpt: The State Department says the entire FY2026 allocation of employment-based second-preference visas for Indian applicants is gone — freezing one of the diaspora's main paths to a green card until the new fiscal year resets the count on October 1.
articles.image_caption: The U.S. Department of State, which confirmed the EB-2 green-card category for India is exhausted for fiscal year 2026
articles.nri_angle: The exhaustion of the EB-2 green-card category for India until October freezes one of the diaspora's main paths to U.S. permanent residency, stranding hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals — many long-time H-1B holders with families and homes — in temporary-visa limbo, and underscoring how the decades-old 7% per-country cap keeps Indian demand permanently mismatched with supply.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian-Origin Mayor Just Became the Most Powerful Kingmaker in Democratic Politics. All Three of His Picks Won.
articles.excerpt: Zohran Mamdani, the son of filmmaker Mira Nair, watched his entire endorsed slate sweep New York's congressional primaries on Tuesday — ousting two sitting members of Congress and signalling that the city's first South Asian mayor now reaches far beyond City Hall.
articles.image_caption: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose three endorsed candidates swept the city's Democratic congressional primaries
articles.nri_angle: Zohran Mamdani — New York's first South Asian mayor and the son of filmmaker Mira Nair — has become a national Democratic kingmaker barely six months into office, showing that an Indian-origin politician can now sit at the centre of American power and reshape a major party, even as his democratic-socialist politics divide a diaspora that is no monolith.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Offering Its Scientists Abroad Up to Rs 60 Lakh a Year to Come Home. The Real Question Is Whether Money Is Enough.
articles.excerpt: The Prime Minister Research Chair Scheme wants 120 Indian-origin researchers back from labs like OpenAI, DeepMind and Anthropic over five years, with grants of up to Rs 5 crore. Applications close July 15 — and the diaspora is doing the maths.
articles.image_caption: India's IITs and IISc anchor the Prime Minister Research Chair Scheme 2026, which seeks to bring Indian-origin researchers home from global labs
articles.nri_angle: The PMRC Scheme 2026 is India's most concrete and generous attempt yet to reverse its brain drain, offering Indian-origin researchers abroad up to Rs 60 lakh a year and Rs 5 crore grants to relocate to the IITs and IISc — putting a specific, deadline-bound offer in front of millions of diaspora scientists, even as the harder questions of lab quality and bureaucratic friction remain unanswered.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Has a New Target in Its Immigration Crackdown: the Lawyers. The First Big Fine Involves Indian Asylum Claims.
articles.excerpt: DHS says it has fined a single attorney more than $255,000 over 64 asylum documents filed mostly for Indian nationals — declarations it calls near-identical. For a community where word-of-mouth lawyers are how many navigate the system, the message lands close to home.
articles.image_caption: U.S. immigration enforcement signage; DHS has begun fining attorneys over allegedly fraudulent asylum filings made largely for Indian nationals
articles.nri_angle: Indians are among the fastest-growing groups seeking U.S. asylum, and DHS's new policy of fining the attorneys behind allegedly fraudulent claims means even genuine applicants tied to a flagged lawyer can see their cases reopened — making it essential for NRIs to verify a lawyer's license and never let anyone fabricate their persecution story.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: From Times Square to the Bund, the World Rolled Out Its Mat Again. India's Quietest Export Just Had Its Biggest Day.
articles.excerpt: The 12th International Day of Yoga drew 35,000 to Kolkata's Red Road and millions across 2,500 venues in more than 210 Indian missions — a single morning in which the diaspora became, for a few hours, India's most visible ambassadors.
articles.image_caption: Participants mark the International Day of Yoga, observed on June 21 across India and more than 2,500 venues worldwide
articles.nri_angle: The International Day of Yoga is one of the few mornings each year when overseas Indians' own culture becomes the main public event in cities from New York to Toronto to Shanghai — a two-way act of belonging, organised by their consulates and open to everyone, that this year's 'Healthy Ageing' theme made quietly personal for a community thinking across continents and generations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Wants to Put an Expiry Date on the Student Visa. India's 363,000 Students Are First in Line.
articles.excerpt: For decades an F-1 visa let you stay as long as you stayed enrolled. A rule that just cleared the White House would swap that for a fixed clock — and every extra year, every job after graduation, would need Washington's sign-off.
articles.image_caption: Students on a US university campus; Indians are now the largest international student group in America, with over 363,000 enrolled in 2024-25
articles.nri_angle: Indian students are the largest international cohort in the United States, and putting a fixed clock on the F-1 visa — with USCIS sign-off needed for extensions and OPT work after graduation — injects fresh bureaucratic risk into the study-work-H-1B-green-card path that NRI families stake their savings on.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Was Born a Parsi and Never Left Her Faith. Because She Married a Hindu, Her Son Can't Set Foot in the Temple.
articles.excerpt: A 1908 ruling decided that only Parsi men could pass on the religion. More than a century later, a mother and her young son are asking India's Supreme Court to undo it — a case that goes to the heart of who gets to belong to one of the world's smallest, oldest communities.
articles.image_caption: A Parsi (Zoroastrian) fire temple in India; a Supreme Court case challenges rules that bar the children of Parsi women who marry outside the faith
articles.nri_angle: Interfaith marriage is even more common in the global Zoroastrian diaspora than in India, so a Supreme Court ruling on whether the children of Parsi women belong to the faith would either give overseas communities' growing inclusion a constitutional foundation or harden a divide already splitting Parsi families across continents.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Firms Shut, 300 Workers Unpaid: Indians and Bangladeshis Turn Up at Singapore's Manpower Ministry
articles.excerpt: Most are owed two months' wages, some as much as $7,000. When their bosses went silent and the worksite was locked, more than a hundred showed up at the ministry's door — a rare public stand in a city that runs on migrant labour.
articles.image_caption: Singapore's Ministry of Manpower, where the unpaid migrant workers sought help over their withheld wages
articles.nri_angle: India and Bangladesh supply much of Singapore's blue-collar workforce, and the unpaid air-conditioning technicians of KPA Engineering and SK Industries are a reminder that migration's most exposed layer feeds directly into the live debate over how origin countries protect their lowest-paid workers abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Indian-American Doctors Just Got One of India's Highest Honours. Both Spent Their Careers Fighting Cancer.
articles.excerpt: At the second Padma investiture in New Delhi, a radiation oncologist from New York and a gastroenterologist from Kansas were honoured — a quiet reminder that the diaspora India celebrates is not only its CEOs and chess prodigies, but its physicians.
articles.image_caption: Dr Dattatreyudu Nori, the Indian-American radiation oncologist awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2026 for his pioneering work in cancer treatment
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin physicians make up roughly one in ten doctors in the United States, and honouring radiation oncologist Dattatreyudu Nori and gastroenterologist Prateek Sharma is India claiming a share of a diaspora legacy that is usually defined by tech CEOs — telling NRI doctors that decades of unflashy clinical work are seen and valued back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Supreme Court Just Made the Green Card a Little Less Secure at the Border
articles.excerpt: In a 6-3 ruling, the justices said immigration officers don't need clear evidence of a crime to treat a returning permanent resident as someone newly 'seeking admission' — a quiet shift with outsized stakes for the millions of Indians who hold green cards and travel home.
articles.image_caption: The United States Supreme Court, which ruled 6-3 in Blanche v. Lau that border officers need not have clear evidence of a crime to treat a returning green-card holder as an applicant for admission
articles.nri_angle: Indians are among the largest groups of US green-card holders and applicants, and for a community whose life revolves around trips home for weddings, festivals and family emergencies, the ruling makes re-entry riskier for any permanent resident with even a minor or old criminal matter — prompting attorneys to urge affected NRIs to seek legal advice before travelling internationally.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Canada Is About to Spend Half a Trillion on Defence. It Wants India to Build a Lot of It.
articles.excerpt: Ottawa's military budget is on a 'hockey stick' toward 5% of GDP, and its envoy in New Delhi is openly courting Indian manufacturers — a pairing of Canadian technology and Indian scale that, just two years after a bitter diplomatic rupture, signals how far the relationship has swung back.
articles.image_caption: A Royal Canadian Air Force CF-18 Hornet; Canada is courting Indian defence and aerospace manufacturers as its military budget climbs toward 5% of GDP
articles.nri_angle: For the 1.8-million-strong Indo-Canadian community that lived through the Nijjar-era diplomatic freeze, a half-trillion-dollar Canadian defence build-up courting Indian manufacturers is the strongest sign yet that the two governments are rebuilding ties on durable foundations of shared industry and security — with potential jobs and contracts in Indo-Canadian aerospace hubs around Montreal and Toronto.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Kohli's Name Is on India's England Squad. Whether He Boards the Plane Is Another Question.
articles.excerpt: The BCCI has named a 15-man ODI squad for next month's tour of England, with Shubman Gill leading, Jasprit Bumrah back, and Virat Kohli picked subject to a fitness check on the hamstring that troubled him in the IPL final — a selection the diaspora will be watching closer than most.
articles.image_caption: Virat Kohli, whose inclusion in India's ODI squad for the England tour is subject to a fitness check on a hamstring strain from the IPL 2026 final
articles.nri_angle: An India tour of England is a home-from-home event for Britain's large Indian-origin community, turning grounds like Edgbaston and Old Trafford into seas of blue, while diaspora fans across North America and the Gulf watch through the night — and Kohli's fitness saga, Gill's new captaincy and the road to the 2027 World Cup make every selection call matter to millions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Isn't at the World Cup. But Three Players of Indian Descent Are.
articles.excerpt: For the first time, three footballers of Indian heritage — New Zealand's Sarpreet Singh, Qatar's Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid and Australia's Nishan Velupillay — are playing at a men's World Cup simultaneously, carrying a diaspora's story onto the sport's biggest stage even as India watches from the outside.
articles.image_caption: Sarpreet Singh, the New Zealand midfielder born in Auckland to a family from Jalandhar, Punjab — believed to be the first Sikh footballer at a men's World Cup
articles.nri_angle: For a diaspora of some 35 million that has never seen India at a men's World Cup, the simultaneous presence of three Indian-origin players — a Punjabi Sikh for New Zealand, a Gulf-born Malayali for Qatar, and a South-Asian-heritage winger for Australia — is both a source of pride and a pointed reminder of the talent India fails to develop at home, making the 2026 tournament a uniquely personal watch for Indians worldwide.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Newest Mega-Airport Is About to Send Its First Plane Abroad. The Destination Is Abu Dhabi.
articles.excerpt: On July 15, Air India Express will fly Navi Mumbai International Airport's maiden international service to Abu Dhabi — the moment a greenfield giant meant to relieve Mumbai's choked skies joins the global map, and a new door home for the Gulf's vast Indian workforce.
articles.image_caption: Navi Mumbai International Airport, which will operate its first international flight — an Air India Express service to Abu Dhabi (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For the Gulf's vast Indian workforce — the UAE hosts one of the world's largest Indian expatriate communities and a major source of India's record remittances — Navi Mumbai's first international flight opens another, less-congested gateway home and is set to deepen the Mumbai-to-Abu Dhabi ties of investment, family travel and business that define modern diaspora life.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Trump's Trade Envoy Has Left Delhi. India Says the Two Sides Are Now Mapping the Way to a Deal.
articles.excerpt: Two days of talks between US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal ended Wednesday with both governments calling it 'substantial progress' — and Washington saying the long-promised deal is 'very, very close.' What India wants is a tariff edge over its rivals before a July 24 clock runs out.
articles.image_caption: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who led India's side of the two-day trade talks with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in New Delhi
articles.nri_angle: For the millions of Indian-Americans and the diaspora-run importers, distributors and tech firms that straddle both economies, the tariff line in this deal decides whether Indian-made goods stay competitive on US shelves and whether the talent-mobility and digital-trade chapters ease the careers of engineers and founders working across Silicon Valley and India — with a July 24 deadline raising the stakes of getting it done.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After Two Decades of Talking, India and Europe Finally Have a Date. The 'Mother of All Deals' Gets Signed by December.
articles.excerpt: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal says the India-EU free-trade pact will be signed by December and take effect by February or March 2027, opening nearly the entire European market to Indian exporters — and reshaping the economics for a diaspora that straddles both.
articles.image_caption: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who confirmed the India-EU free-trade pact will be signed by December and take effect by early 2027
articles.nri_angle: For the millions of people of Indian origin across Europe, the FTA promises cheaper costs and wider margins for diaspora-run businesses that trade Indian textiles, food and craft goods, more predictable export routes into a 450-million-consumer market, and clearer professional-mobility rules for skilled Indians eyeing the continent as US and UK routes grow uncertain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: China Just Got the WTO to Put India's 'Make in India' Solar Push on Trial
articles.excerpt: Geneva's Dispute Settlement Body has agreed to set up a panel to examine India's tariffs and incentives for solar and IT goods, which Beijing says discriminate against Chinese products — a test case for how far India can go to build factories at home without breaking global trade rules.
articles.image_caption: A solar installation; China has won a WTO panel to examine India's solar and IT-goods tariffs and incentives
articles.nri_angle: The case puts 'Make in India' — the manufacturing drive that has drawn diaspora capital, returning engineers and NRI investors betting on Indian factories — on trial at the WTO, testing whether India can keep using tariffs and local-content incentives to build a China-alternative industrial base without breaking global trade rules.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Quietly Telling the Gulf to Pay Its 5 Million Workers More. It's a Billion-Dollar Bet With a Catch.
articles.excerpt: Over the past several months, Indian diplomats across all six Gulf states have sharply raised the minimum salaries they recommend for Indian workers — a drive that could pull in billions more in remittances, but also risks pricing some of India's own citizens out of the market.
articles.image_caption: Construction in the Gulf, where more than five million Indians work and remit billions home
articles.nri_angle: More than five million Indians — the largest migrant group in the Gulf and the source of remittances that sustain countless households across Kerala, UP, Bihar and Tamil Nadu — stand to earn meaningfully more if India's push to raise minimum wages succeeds, but blue-collar workers are also the ones who could lose jobs if Gulf employers pivot to cheaper labour from rival nations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: On July 15, an Indian Professional Posted to Britain Stops Paying Twice for the Same Pension
articles.excerpt: The India-UK free-trade pact, signed last year, finally goes live next month — and tucked inside it is a social-security carve-out that puts real money back in the pockets of Indians sent to work in Britain. Trade Minister Piyush Goyal flies to London this week to nail down the rollout.
articles.image_caption: The City of London; the India-UK CETA free-trade pact comes into force on July 15, easing trade and professional mobility
articles.nri_angle: Britain's 1.9-million-strong Indian community — and especially the IT engineers, consultants and managers posted there temporarily by Indian firms — gain real take-home pay from July 15, when the India-UK CETA's Double Contribution Convention stops them paying social security in both countries, while diaspora-run exporters get new openings into the British market.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: One of India's Biggest Automakers Woke Up to a Ransomware Attack. The Bigger Worry Is What It Signals.
articles.excerpt: Bajaj Auto, the Pune-based maker of motorcycles and three-wheelers sold from Lagos to Los Angeles, says a ransomware attack hit its systems and those of its technology arm early on June 23. It calls its response successful so far — but the breach lands amid a wave of cyberattacks on India's industrial backbone.
articles.image_caption: Bajaj Auto, the Pune-based maker of motorcycles and three-wheelers, disclosed a ransomware attack on its systems
articles.nri_angle: Bajaj is a globally recognised Indian brand whose two- and three-wheelers are sold across the diaspora's home markets in Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and a stock many NRIs hold; a ransomware hit on so digitised a manufacturer is a warning sign about the cyber-resilience of the Indian industrial firms the diaspora invests in and takes pride in.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Britain Is About to Smash Its June Heat Record. For 1.9 Million Indians There, This Is a Safety Story.
articles.excerpt: A Saharan 'heat dome' has pushed western Europe into a deadly, record-breaking heatwave. The UK Met Office has issued a rare red alert warning of a risk to life, schools are shutting and trains are cancelled — just as London hosts its flagship climate week and changes prime ministers.
articles.image_caption: The City of London skyline; Britain is forecast to break its June heat record amid a rare Met Office red alert
articles.nri_angle: Britain's 1.9 million people of Indian origin — concentrated in heat-exposed cities, often in older homes without air-conditioning, with elderly relatives in the at-risk group — are living through a record, potentially deadly heatwave, making this an urgent safety story for the UK and wider European diaspora, complete with the official guidance families need.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Their Lawmakers Have a Message for 5 Million Indian-Americans: Stop Being on the Menu, Get a Seat at the Table.
articles.excerpt: At a Capitol Hill gathering, Congressmen Raja Krishnamoorthi, Suhas Subramanyam and Shri Thanedar urged Indian-Americans to run for office at every level as anti-Hindu and anti-India hate rises — a call for one of America's wealthiest and most-educated communities to convert economic clout into political power.
articles.image_caption: Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, who urged Indian-Americans to run for office at every level
articles.nri_angle: This is a direct call to the 5.2-million-strong Indian-American community to convert its economic and educational success into political representation, framed by its own elected lawmakers as the only durable defence against rising anti-Hindu and anti-India hate and against stalled priorities like the green-card backlog.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Will Now Let Its Banks Lend NRIs Money to Buy More Indian Deposits. The Returns Could Touch 15%.
articles.excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has cleared domestic lenders to extend loans to non-residents against their foreign-currency deposits — including through GIFT City — the final missing piece of a scheme designed to pull diaspora dollars in and prop up a weak rupee. Analysts say leverage could lift NRI returns toward 12-15 percent and draw in tens of billions.
articles.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India, which cleared banks to lend to NRIs against their foreign-currency deposits
articles.nri_angle: This is aimed squarely at non-resident Indians: the RBI is now letting banks lend NRIs money against their own dollar deposits, a leverage loop that analysts say could push diaspora returns toward 12-15 percent while channelling tens of billions of overseas-Indian dollars back home to steady the rupee.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Mounting Its Biggest-Ever Security Operation for the Amarnath Pilgrimage. Here's Why This Year Is Different.
articles.excerpt: Ahead of the 57-day Amarnath Yatra that begins July 3, the government has approved a record 670 companies of central forces — a multi-layered grid stretching from the Jammu gateway to the Himalayan cave shrine. For the diaspora that travels home for the pilgrimage, and for families across Kashmir, the scale of this year's deployment is unprecedented.
articles.image_caption: Security personnel guard pilgrims at the Amarnath cave shrine in Jammu and Kashmir; this year India is mounting its largest-ever security operation for the Yatra (Wikimedia Commons).
articles.nri_angle: The Amarnath Yatra draws NRIs who fly home each summer for the pilgrimage and is watched closely by the large Kashmiri and J&K-origin diaspora, so a record 670-company security deployment for the July 3-August 28 Yatra matters both as the safety guarantee that makes the trip possible and as a barometer of how their home region is being governed.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Becoming an American Is About to Get Much More Expensive. Indian Green-Card Holders Will Feel It First.
articles.excerpt: A new Trump administration proposal would raise the cost of applying for US citizenship by up to 80 percent — from $710 to $1,280 online, and $760 to $1,330 on paper — while scrapping most fee waivers for low-income applicants. For the hundreds of thousands of Indians who form the largest single bloc of new American citizens, the math on naturalization just changed.
articles.image_caption: A US naturalization ceremony; a new DHS proposal would raise citizenship application fees by up to 80 percent
articles.nri_angle: Indians are consistently among the largest groups of new US citizens and the biggest bloc on employment-based green-card tracks, so a proposed 75-80% jump in the N-400 naturalization fee — toward roughly ₹1.26 lakh per applicant — plus the loss of low-income waivers directly raises the cost of the final step for hundreds of thousands of NRI families, with a 60-day comment window before any rule becomes final.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After Six Decades, India Is Letting Private Money Into Its Nuclear Plants
articles.excerpt: A landmark law has ended the state monopoly on atomic power, opening the sector to private operators and up to 49% foreign investment. New Delhi is chasing roughly $26 billion in private capital and a 100-gigawatt target — and a diaspora hungry for both clean-energy bets and a stake in India's rise is squarely in the frame.
articles.image_caption: Technicians load fuel assemblies at the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant; India has opened the sector to private operators and foreign investment for the first time
articles.nri_angle: The opening of India's nuclear sector gives overseas Indians a first-ever, ground-floor route into one of the country's biggest long-term infrastructure bets — a patient clean-energy play suited to diaspora capital, foreign partners and the many NRIs working in global nuclear, engineering and clean-tech — while answering a diaspora desire for Indian energy security after the recent Hormuz oil scare.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indians in the UAE Have a Five-Day Window to Sort Their Passports. Then Services Go Dark.
articles.excerpt: The Indian Embassy is pausing all routine passport, visa and attestation work from June 26 to 30 as a new contractor, Al Hind Tours, replaces BLS and SGIVS from July 1. For the roughly 3.5 million Indians in the UAE — the country's largest expatriate community — the message is simple: file now, or wait until July.
articles.image_caption: An Indian Emergency Certificate, a consular travel document issued by Indian missions abroad; UAE consular services pause June 26-30 during a contractor handover
articles.nri_angle: The UAE hosts India's single largest overseas community of roughly 3.5 million people, so a planned five-day pause in passport, visa and attestation services — with a hard June 25 filing deadline before Al Hind Tours replaces BLS and SGIVS on July 1 — directly affects thousands of NRI households, especially blue-collar workers whose jobs, tenancies and family visas hinge on timely consular paperwork.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ambani Just Filed the Paperwork for India's Biggest-Ever IPO. The Company Is Jio.
articles.excerpt: Reliance has lodged draft papers to list Jio Platforms in Mumbai in an offering that could raise about $4 billion and value the business near $137 billion. For a diaspora that already touches Jio through Meta and Google's stakes, it is a rare chance to own a slice of the network that rewired India.
articles.image_caption: Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, whose Jio Platforms has filed for India's largest-ever IPO
articles.nri_angle: The Jio IPO gives overseas Indians a rare, direct way to own the network that rewired daily life back home — the cheap data behind their video calls, the rails behind their remittances, the streaming that keeps them tied to Indian cricket and cinema — and, through the NRI investor route, the listing will be a marquee test of whether diaspora appetite for Indian assets holds up in a jittery market.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Got Its First Sovereign-AI Unicorn. The Bigger Question Is Whether It's Building Fast Enough.
articles.excerpt: Bengaluru's Sarvam has raised $234 million to build AI models from scratch in India, even as a Wall Street note warns the country risks letting foreign systems power its banks, defence and public services. For a diaspora that staffs the world's AI labs, the contest over who controls the models is suddenly personal.
articles.image_caption: A data-center server hall; India is racing to build sovereign AI models trained at home
articles.nri_angle: Indians and people of Indian origin run or sit near the top of nearly every major AI lab in the United States — the very talent that built the frontier models India now worries about depending on — so India's sovereign-AI push is an attempt to give that diaspora a reason to build at home or for home, even as many NRIs work for the Western labs whose dominance New Delhi is trying to reduce.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Rescue Plan for 11,000 Stranded Sailors Is Now Underway in the Gulf. Many of Them Are Indian.
articles.excerpt: The UN's shipping agency said on Tuesday it has begun contacting hundreds of vessels trapped behind the Strait of Hormuz to start evacuating some 11,000 seafarers, after the US-Iran ceasefire reopened a path through the waterway. For the world's largest single supplier of merchant sailors, the operation is intensely personal.
articles.image_caption: An oil tanker at sea; the IMO has begun evacuating some 11,000 seafarers stranded behind the Strait of Hormuz (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indians are the single largest nationality in the global merchant marine — well over 250,000 serving seafarers — so a UN operation to evacuate the ~11,000 crew stranded behind the Strait of Hormuz is, for India's coastal communities, a story about their own sons and the remittances that sustain their families, and a reminder that Indian labour crews the ships carrying the world's oil just as visibly as it staffs Silicon Valley and the NHS.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Monsoon Is Running 43% Short, and the Government Is Drawing Up Plans for 300 Districts
articles.excerpt: With rains the weakest in over a decade and the weather office warning of an El Nino-stunted season, New Delhi has put more than 300 farm districts on a contingency footing. For a diaspora bound to rural India by remittances and family land, a thin monsoon is more than a weather story — it is a livelihood story.
articles.image_caption: A farmer in an Indian paddy field; the 2026 monsoon is running about 43% below average
articles.nri_angle: A failing monsoon hits the diaspora indirectly but unmistakably — the families that NRIs support with over $100 billion in annual remittances are concentrated in rain-fed farming districts, so a poor harvest raises remittance demand even as food inflation pressures the rupee in which overseas Indians hold deposits and send money home, while the climate trajectory of Indian agriculture increasingly shapes the plans of diaspora families who own land back home or are weighing a return.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: For the First Time Since 1973, Congress Has Told a President to End a War. The War Is With Iran.
articles.excerpt: The US Senate voted 50-48 on Tuesday to direct Donald Trump to pull American forces out of the conflict with Iran — the first time both chambers have passed such a resolution since the War Powers Act became law. It is likely symbolic. But for a diaspora that watched this war whipsaw oil prices, flights home and the safety of thousands of Indians in the Gulf, the vote is a signal worth reading.
articles.image_caption: The US Senate; lawmakers voted 50-48 to direct President Trump to halt military action against Iran
articles.nri_angle: The war this resolution targets reached deep into diaspora life — whipsawing oil prices and the rupee, threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, leaving nearly 18,000 Indian seafarers trapped in Gulf waters and forcing the evacuation of 1,700 citizens — so a bipartisan Senate signal that Washington wants the conflict to end speaks directly to the energy security, currency stability and Gulf livelihoods that millions of Indian families abroad depend on.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Japan's New PM Makes Her First India Trip Next Week — With 50 Company Bosses and a Shopping List of Chips
articles.excerpt: Sanae Takaichi's debut visit to India from July 1-3 will now be held in New Delhi after a planned summit in Guwahati was shelved over a tight schedule. Behind the venue shuffle sits a far bigger story: a Japanese business armada and an India-Japan agenda built around semiconductors, critical minerals and the movement of skilled people — all of which run straight through the diaspora.
articles.image_caption: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who makes her first official visit to India from July 1-3
articles.nri_angle: Japan, racing to build out semiconductors and advanced manufacturing while its own workforce shrinks, has been opening doors to skilled Indian engineers, technicians and care workers — so a summit that deepens India-Japan tech, talent-mobility and supply-chain ties opens a fresh destination for diaspora professionals beyond the usual US/UK/Canada/Gulf routes, while Japanese investment into Indian chip and clean-energy projects strengthens the home economy that NRIs stay tethered to through remittances and return migration.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Market Rally Just Hit a Wall. The Warning Sign Wasn't Oil — It Was the Monsoon.
articles.excerpt: The Sensex tumbled 893 points and the Nifty fell 1.16% on Tuesday, snapping a seven-session rally, after a survey showed private-sector growth cooling to a three-month low and a patchy monsoon spooked investors. For diaspora investors who watch Indian equities and the rupee, it was a reminder of how fast the mood can turn.
articles.image_caption: India's stock market; the Sensex fell 893 points on Tuesday, snapping a seven-session rally
articles.nri_angle: NRIs hold Indian equities directly, through funds, and via the NRI deposit routes banks (and the RBI) have been pushing to shore up the rupee — so a sell-off driven by a slowing IT sector, Fed-hike fears and a weak monsoon speaks straight to diaspora portfolios, where the rupee's path determines how far remittances stretch and what Indian assets are worth in dollars.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A US Court Just Cleared the Way to Deport People From Anywhere in America — Without a Judge
articles.excerpt: A divided federal appeals court has revived the Trump administration's power to fast-track deportations of undocumented immigrants found anywhere in the country, not just at the border. The two-year test at the centre of the ruling is exactly where visa overstays — a quiet but real slice of the Indian story in America — are most exposed.
articles.image_caption: US immigration enforcement; a divided appeals court revived nationwide fast-track deportations
articles.nri_angle: The revived policy turns on a two-year continuous-presence test enforced anywhere in the US — the exact zone where Indian visa overstays (lapsed F-1s, expired H-1Bs, overstayed visitor visas) are most exposed, making current documentation and proof of time in the country an urgent priority for anyone in or near a status gap, and reshaping the calculus for mixed-status diaspora families who can no longer count on the slow immigration-court backlog.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Isn't Just the World's Biggest Source of Skilled Migrants. Its Workers Now Out-Earn the Locals.
articles.excerpt: New global talent data puts India at the very top of the skilled-migration map — the number-one source of US H-1B hires and a leading feeder for UK skilled-worker visas and EU Blue Cards. The twist that reframes the whole 'cheap labour' debate: Indian hires abroad are increasingly commanding a wage premium over comparable local workers, not a discount.
articles.image_caption: The Infosys campus in India; Indian skilled migrants now out-earn locals in top destinations (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The finding that Indian skilled migrants out-earn local workers is a direct rebuttal to the 'cheap labour' narrative that shapes the visa rules, fee hikes and public mood diaspora families live under — and, with the Gulf, Australia and Canada now actively courting Indian talent and India itself drawing senior professionals home, it reframes the career map facing the diaspora's next generation from a one-way exit into a position of genuine leverage.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: UK-India Week Just Opened at Warwick — and the Real Action Is a Gujarat-to-West-Midlands Handshake
articles.excerpt: The 10th edition of UK-India Week, the biggest event in the bilateral calendar, opened at the University of Warwick with a state-to-region pitch: a Gujarat delegation courting the West Midlands on advanced manufacturing, clean energy, life sciences and skills — a model that turns broad diplomacy into concrete, place-to-place partnerships.
articles.image_caption: The University of Warwick, host of the 10th UK-India Week, where a Gujarat delegation courted the West Midlands
articles.nri_angle: The West Midlands is a heartland of Britain's ~1.9 million-strong Indian community — much of it Gujarati, concentrated in Birmingham, Leicester and Coventry — so a formal Gujarat–West Midlands partnership turns the diaspora's ancestral state and adopted region into business partners, formalising the connective role Gujarati families have played in UK-India trade for generations and giving diaspora entrepreneurs a direct bridge between Gujarat's investment incentives and British innovation ecosystems.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Drug Regulator Just Flagged 159 Medicines as Substandard. Some Are Drugs You Take Every Day.
articles.excerpt: In its latest monthly check, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation declared 159 samples 'Not of Standard Quality' and one outright spurious — covering common blood-pressure pills, diabetes tablets, antibiotics and vitamin supplements made by household-name companies. For a diaspora that treats India as its pharmacy, the list is a recurring uncomfortable read.
articles.image_caption: A pile of medicine tablets; India's drug regulator flagged 159 drug samples as Not of Standard Quality in its latest monthly alert
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs treat India as their pharmacy — stocking up on blood-pressure pills, diabetes drugs, antibiotics and supplements on visits home or having relatives ship them abroad for a fraction of Western prices — so a monthly list of substandard and spurious medicines is a direct, practical health-safety concern for diaspora families and the ageing parents they manage from afar.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adani Just Opened an Airport in the Heart of Kutch. For the Gujarati Diaspora, It's a New Door Home.
articles.excerpt: The Mundra Airport in Gujarat began scheduled passenger flights on Tuesday via regional carrier Star Air — connecting the remote Kutch region directly to Mumbai, Goa and six other cities — as the Adani Group unveiled plans to invest about Rs 1 lakh crore across its airports over the next five years.
articles.image_caption: A Star Air Embraer regional jet; Star Air launched the first scheduled passenger flights from Adani Mundra Airport in Gujarat
articles.nri_angle: Kutch and Gujarat are the ancestral home of one of the largest, most prosperous Indian diasporas — communities in East Africa, the UK, US and Gulf with deep family, property and trade ties to the district — so a direct-flight airport at Mundra removes the awkward final leg of every trip home and strengthens the port-SEZ-airport logistics hub that NRI entrepreneurs watch closely.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Dream Degree Abroad Is Getting Too Expensive and Too Risky. Indian Families Are Doing the Math.
articles.excerpt: A rupee that has lost more than a tenth of its value in a year, visa crackdowns from Washington to Ottawa, and a job market that no longer pays off the loan — the calculus that sent a generation of Indians to the West is breaking down, and the September intake is already shrinking.
articles.image_caption: Graduates celebrate at a university commencement in South Asia. For many families, a foreign degree remains the aspiration even as costs and visa risks climb.
articles.nri_angle: Sending a child to study in the West is the biggest financial bet most Indian middle-class and NRI families make, so a falling rupee, visa crackdowns and a broken post-graduation job market turn that bet into a potential debt trap — and increasingly the diaspora's relatives abroad are the co-signers and safety net when the loans outrun gig-economy earnings.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
